posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring post from a CRO articulating the exact compliance/explainability pain Milo solves, with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the trust gap with a specific observation and let the insight do the work
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' moment is where a lot of analytics teams are quietly falling apart right now. It's not even about the accuracy — it's that the number exists with no trail behind it. Regulators don't want a correct answer, they want a defensible one. Big difference.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that it's rarely a data problem
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard is almost never the problem. It's that finance teams have been burned before — a number was wrong once, a filter was misconfigured, and now the spreadsheet feels safer because at least they know exactly what they're looking at. You can rebuild the tool a hundred times and it won't fix that. What actually rebuilt the trust for you when it did work, even partially?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add a layer about why dashboards get bloated in the first place, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is usually a political problem dressed up as a data problem. Everyone fought to get their metric on the dashboard, so it became a graveyard of compromises nobody owns. The 10% to 85% jump makes complete sense — people only open tools they actually trust to tell them something. The real question is how you stop the next stakeholder from adding metric number 6.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at a retail brand is engaging on a post about BI chaos and lack of data ownership — validate the 'who owns truth' framing with a sharper observation, add the insight that tooling isn't the problem, definitions are
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing is so common it's almost a rite of passage. Everyone assumes the problem is access to data — but the real problem is that nobody did the boring work of agreeing what the data *means* before handing out licenses. The tool becomes a mirror for organisational dysfunction, not a solution to it. Who owns the definition, not just the dashboard?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as a security risk — validate the framing with a sharper operational angle, with a CEO at a 90-person data company watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think most analytics vendors have caught up to it yet. A hallucinated number in a dashboard isn't just wrong — it's an unsigned input that bypassed every control your team spent years building. We obsess over who can access the data, but almost nobody is auditing what the AI is actually claiming the data says. How many orgs even have a review process for AI-generated outputs before they hit a decision-maker?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: COO at Sterling Consulting engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-data users — validate the core frustration with a specific observation, add the insight that 'self-service' is a design failure not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: The £200k is almost never the real cost. It's the six months of 'we'll just ask Dave to pull that' before everyone quietly gives up. Self-service failed because most tools were designed so a data person could hand off a dashboard, not so a ops or finance lead could actually explore a question themselves. Wonder how many of those platforms the vendor would still call a success.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company surfacing a data trust/culture problem — validate the real diagnosis, add the layer about what 'culture fix' actually requires in practice
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is almost always the symptom, not the cause — what's usually underneath it is that nobody agreed on what the number was *supposed* to mean before anyone started building dashboards. Culture is the right answer, but in my experience 'culture' in this context just means someone with enough authority finally sits three teams down and makes a decision. The hard part isn't knowing that. It's who actually calls that meeting.

posts.post_text: Enterprise analytics teams are wasting 40% of their time on ad-hoc reporting requests. Our new AI-Powered Analytics eliminates the bottleneck entirely. See how Fortune 500 companies are scaling their data teams with ThoughtSpot. #analytics #enterprise
posts.angle: ThoughtSpot pushing AI-eliminates-bottleneck narrative — challenge with the reality that the bottleneck is trust, not speed
posts.draft_comment: Curious about that 40% figure — in my experience the ad-hoc requests don't stop when you add AI, they multiply, because now everyone thinks the data is easier to get to. The real bottleneck isn't the reporting queue, it's whether the person asking actually trusts the number they get back. Faster answers to the wrong question is still the wrong question.

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the adoption gap in enterprise AI rollouts — validate the shadow AI insight and add the 'knowing what to ask' problem as a data-specific angle worth exploring
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all — 'knowing what to ask' is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that stat. Most people don't have a mental model of what the tool can actually do for their specific job, so they default to nothing or go rogue. The shadow AI piece is the most honest part of this whole story. What does your org actually do when you catch someone using ChatGPT on their phone — slap their wrist or try to understand what need it's meeting?
